source_metadata.title: Switching to Integrase Inhibitors and Cardiovascular Disease Risk in Treatment-Experienced People with HIV: A Sequential Target Trial Emulation in the Swiss HIV Cohort Study
source_metadata.design: Observational sequential target trial emulation using Swiss HIV Cohort Study data
source_metadata.source_scope: Uploaded accepted manuscript; referenced supplemental tables/figures were not included in the 16-page file.

source_inconsistencies.issue: The Results text states n=52 were excluded for not being on ART, whereas Figure 1 states n=53. The reported total of 1,687 exclusions reconciles only with n=53.
source_inconsistencies.handling: No atom was created for the conflicting exclusion subcount; the reported analytic total of 8,815 individuals was retained.

source_inconsistencies.issue: The narrative reports the 6-year ITT adjusted risk-difference 95% CI as -0.49 to 0.50 percentage points, while Table 2 reports -0.49 to 0.58.
source_inconsistencies.handling: The quantitative atom anchored to Table 2 uses -0.49 to 0.58 and the discrepancy is preserved here rather than silently reconciled.

extraction_limitations: The uploaded manuscript references supplemental Tables S1-S9 and Figure S1, but the supplement was not present in the uploaded file; supplemental numerical estimates and detailed protocol fields could not be independently atomized or verified.

Subgroup findings were available only as a narrative statement that no significant interactions were observed; subgroup-specific effect estimates were not present in the uploaded file, so they were represented as a qualitative_result rather than subgroup_result atoms.
No calculated_from_reported_data or extractor_inference atoms were created; quantitative atoms were limited to directly reported or normalized reported values.
All atoms remain review_status=needs_review because no human verification step was performed.

atoms.canonical_statement: The study assessed the effect of switching to INSTI-based ART versus remaining on non-INSTI-based ART on 6-year cardiovascular disease risk among well-controlled people with HIV in the Swiss HIV Cohort Study.

The investigators conducted an observational study emulating a sequence of target trials to estimate intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects of switching to INSTI-based ART on cardiovascular events.
Repeated target trials were emulated at the start of each calendar month from November 2011 through September 2025.
Individuals could enter multiple sequential trials when they repeatedly met eligibility criteria.
Eligibility required age greater than 18 years.

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligibility required HIV viral suppression of ≤50 copies/mL.

atoms.canonical_statement: Eligibility required current non-INSTI-based ART, defined as at least three antiretrovirals from at least two classes or protease-inhibitor-based dual therapy.

atoms.canonical_statement: The intervention strategy was INSTI-based ART, defined as an ART combination containing at least one integrase strand transfer inhibitor.

exposures.details: ART combination including at least one integrase strand transfer inhibitor

atoms.canonical_statement: The cardiovascular disease outcome was the first myocardial infarction, stroke, or invasive cardiovascular procedure during up to 6 years of follow-up.

outcome.definition: First occurrence of myocardial infarction, stroke, or an invasive cardiovascular procedure
outcome.measurement_method: Centrally validated using standardized algorithms; adjudicated blinded to ART history

atoms.canonical_statement: The emulation used the Swiss HIV Cohort Study, an ongoing prospective cohort reported to include approximately 72% of people receiving ART in Switzerland.
SHCS follow-up occurred at 6-month intervals for about 90% of participants and 12-month intervals for about 10%; cardiovascular events were centrally validated and adjudicated blinded to ART history.
The intention-to-treat analysis emulated 167 monthly trials and used pooled logistic regression on a person-month dataset.
Time-varying characteristics were carried forward between cohort visits, and missing data were treated as distinct categories.

The intention-to-treat outcome model adjusted for baseline demographic, HIV-related, cardiovascular risk, renal, medication, and calendar-time covariates and included treatment-by-time interactions with linear and quadratic time terms.
In the per-protocol analysis, participants were artificially censored when they switched to the alternative treatment strategy or stopped ART for more than two months.
The per-protocol analysis used time-varying non-stabilized inverse probability weights for treatment non-adherence and other censoring, with final weights truncated at the 99th percentile.
Population-average treatment effects were expressed as adjusted risk ratios and adjusted risk differences with 95% confidence intervals from 200 non-parametric bootstrap samples.

Exploratory effect-modification analyses considered sex, age below versus at least 65 years, and baseline abacavir use; interaction p-values below 0.1 were considered suggestive of effect modification.
A sensitivity analysis excluded raltegravir initiators and censored individuals at raltegravir switch because raltegravir had initially been used as rescue therapy.
A total of 8,815 individuals were included in the analysis and contributed 539,017 person-trials; 533,267 person-trials were assigned to non-INSTI ART and 5,750 to INSTI-based ART.

population.label: Included SHCS analytic population
inclusion_criteria: Receiving non-INSTI-based ART at trial baseline

atoms.canonical_statement: Across sequential trial baselines, median age was 48 years (IQR 41–55), median time on ART was 11 years (IQR 6–16), and median CD4 count was 631 cells/µL (IQR 473–826).

population.label: Included SHCS analytic population
inclusion_criteria: Receiving non-INSTI-based ART at trial baseline

atoms.canonical_statement: Tenofovir alafenamide use (31.4% vs 15.9%) and abacavir use (33.1% vs 20.2%) were more frequent among person-trials switching to INSTI-based ART than among those remaining on non-INSTI ART.
Among 5,750 INSTI switchers, 56.8% received dolutegravir, 17.9% elvitegravir, 12.3% bictegravir, 11.8% raltegravir, and 1.2% cabotegravir.
During follow-up, 963 individuals switched from an INSTI-based regimen back to non-INSTI-based ART.
In the intention-to-treat analysis, 507 cardiovascular events occurred among individuals: 145 myocardial infarctions, 125 strokes, and 237 invasive cardiovascular procedures.
In the per-protocol analysis, 462 cardiovascular events were recorded; across sequential trials these corresponded to 10,943 events in the non-INSTI arm and 197 in the INSTI arm.
At 1 year, the intention-to-treat adjusted risk ratio for cardiovascular disease with switching to INSTI-based ART versus remaining on non-INSTI ART was 1.34 (95% CI 1.03–1.69).

atoms.canonical_statement: No significant interaction was observed between treatment strategy and age, sex, or baseline abacavir use.
Results were unchanged when individuals were censored at raltegravir start, indicating that the findings were not driven solely by raltegravir use.
Average weight gain one year after switching to an INSTI-based regimen was 1.2 kg.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors concluded that switching to INSTI-based ART in routine Swiss practice did not increase long-term cardiovascular disease risk in people with well-controlled HIV.
The authors concluded that the early increase in absolute cardiovascular risk after switching was small in magnitude.
The intervention was defined at the INSTI class level rather than by individual INSTI drug, so drug-specific cardiovascular effects were not disentangled.
Because ART consists of drug combinations, co-administered agents could influence cardiovascular risk; baseline abacavir use was adjusted for, but individual drug effects were not isolated.
As an observational analysis, the study remained vulnerable to unmeasured confounding; lifestyle factors and aspects of clinician-patient switching decisions were not captured.

The Swiss HIV Cohort Study and project were supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation, and Frédérique Chammartin was supported by a Moritz Straus Foundation career grant; the funders reportedly had no role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation, or report writing.
The manuscript reported no conflicts of interest.
Individual-level SHCS data are not openly available because of consent, privacy, and Swiss legal constraints; requests for selected data may be considered by the SHCS Scientific Board and study team.
Scripts to reproduce the analysis were reported as available in a public GitHub repository.
